newsitem.title: USA: Lasers could revolutionize cancer tests, research.
newsitem.headline: Lasers could revolutionize cancer tests, research.

text.p: A simple new point-and-shoot laser technique can pluck out suspicious cells from tissue samples in eight seconds, giving researchers a new tool and raising the possibility of pinpointing cancers as they are forming, researchers said on Thursday.

"Having this technique is the difference between being able to investigate a crime in progress and going back two weeks later to the scene of the crime when much of the evidence has vanished, as we typically do now," said Dr. Lance Liotta, a National Cancer Institute (NCI) researcher and co-author of the report in the journal Science on Friday.

The NCI is starting pilot projects in the research lab, where scientists want to study the inner workings of a diseased cell, and in the clinic, where the technique could give rise to better diagnosis and possibly ways of determining what treatments might work best for a specific tumour and how aggressively to conduct treatment.
"We had no way of easily separating out the diseased cells from the surrounding sea of cells," Liotta said in a telephone interview.

The new method uses an ordinary laboratory microscope, a low energy laser much like the little red pointers used by lecturers, and a film that despite its high-tech name -- transparent ethylene vinyl acetate polymer thermoplastic film -- is basically the same stuff that seals a yogurt container.

The biopsy is placed under a microscope with the film placed on it. A scientist who spots some suspicious cells among the hundreds of cells in the biopsy can push a button on the microscope to activate the laser.

The beam of light passes through the film and focuses on the desired cells. In the process it heats the plastic film, giving it a stickiness like scotch tape. The cells stick to the film, and they can then be analysed.

"We wanted an instrument any scientists could sit down and use immediately,' said Dr. Mike Emmert-Buck, another NCI researcher on the project. "This lets us see a few abnormal looking cells and see thousands of genes at once, look at the nucleus and the protein machinery of the cells."
The scientists have tested it successfully on a variety of cancerous or precancerous cells.
